# The Instanton Representation of Plebanski Gravity: Constraint Preservation Without the Dirac Procedure

## Background and Motivation

The instanton representation of Plebanski gravity provides an alternative phase space formulation of general relativity, distinguished by its treatment of the fundamental field variables and its geometric structure. Within this framework, the equations of motion that emerge from the Plebanski action take on a particular character: they decompose naturally into two distinct components. The first is a **Hodge self-duality condition**, which constrains the curvature of the theory's connection to be self-dual (or, more generally, algebraically special) with respect to an appropriately defined Hodge star operation. The second component consists of a set of **generalized Maxwell's equations**, structurally analogous to the source-free Maxwell equations of electromagnetism, but generalized to accommodate the non-Abelian and gravitational character of the theory.

These equations of motion do not exist in isolation; rather, their consistency and physical viability are intimately tied to the **initial value constraints** of general relativity — namely the Gauss law (reflecting the gauge symmetry of the internal frame), the diffeomorphism (vector) constraint, and the Hamiltonian (scalar) constraint. These constraints encode the true gravitational degrees of freedom of the theory and must be satisfied on an initial spatial slice for the resulting spacetime to correspond to a genuine solution of Einstein's equations. A central question in any constrained Hamiltonian system — and one of paramount importance for gravity — is whether these constraints, once imposed, remain satisfied throughout the entire time evolution generated by the equations of motion. If they did not, the constraint surface would not be preserved, and the theory would fail to consistently propagate the correct number of physical degrees of freedom.

## Main Result: Preservation of the Constraint Surface

The central result of this paper is a rigorous demonstration that the constraint surface — defined as the locus in phase space where the Gauss, diffeomorphism, and Hamiltonian constraints all vanish — is **preserved under the time evolution** dictated by the equations of motion of the instanton representation. In other words, it is shown explicitly that if the initial value constraints are satisfied on some initial hypersurface, then the dynamical evolution generated by the self-duality condition and the generalized Maxwell's equations will preserve this property at all later times. This establishes the internal consistency of the instanton representation as a legitimate and self-contained formulation of general relativity, ensuring that the constraints do not develop secondary inconsistencies or require additional tertiary constraints that could potentially over-constrain or otherwise alter the physical content of the theory.

## Methodology: A Lagrangian Approach to Constraint Preservation

What distinguishes the approach taken in this paper from the standard treatment of constrained systems is the **method by which constraint preservation is established**. In the conventional treatment of constrained Hamiltonian systems — as pioneered by Dirac — one proceeds by computing the Poisson brackets of the constraints with the total Hamiltonian (itself typically expressed as a linear combination of the constraints, augmented by Lagrange multipliers). Consistency then requires that the time derivatives of the constraints, computed via these Poisson brackets, vanish weakly (i.e., on the constraint surface itself), potentially leading to secondary constraints if this is not automatically satisfied.

In marked contrast, the present work establishes the preservation of the constraint surface by working directly with the **Lagrangian equations of motion** — that is, the Hodge self-duality condition and the generalized Maxwell's equations obtained directly from the Plebanski action — rather than invoking the Dirac–Bergmann algorithm with its associated machinery of Poisson brackets, Legendre transforms, and phase space extension. This alternative route offers several conceptual and practical advantages: it circumvents the sometimes cumbersome identification of primary and secondary constraints, avoids potential ambiguities associated with the choice of canonical variables and the construction of the total Hamiltonian, and instead demonstrates constraint preservation as a direct consequence of the structure of the equations of motion themselves. This provides a complementary and, in some respects, more transparent verification of the consistency of the theory, one that is rooted directly in the dynamical content of the action principle rather than in the auxiliary constructions of the canonical formalism.

## Comparative Context: Relation to the Ashtekar Formulation

To situate these results within the broader landscape of connection-based approaches to gravity, the paper concludes with a detailed **comparison to the Ashtekar formulation** of general relativity. The Ashtekar variables — comprising a self-dual (or complex) SU(2) connection and a densitized triad — represent the historically foundational reformulation of general relativity that first demonstrated the utility of connection-dynamics variables in simplifying the constraint structure of the gravitational phase space, and which paved the way for subsequent developments including loop quantum gravity.

By juxtaposing the instanton representation with the Ashtekar formalism, the paper clarifies both the similarities and the essential differences between the two approaches: their treatment of the self-duality condition, the structural form of their respective constraints, and the manner in which the reality conditions and gravitational degrees of freedom are encoded. This comparison serves not only to validate the instanton representation as a consistent and geometrically well-motivated alternative to the Ashtekar formulation, but also to illuminate the broader conceptual relationships between different connection-dynamic formulations of general relativity, thereby situating the paper's results within the appropriate historical and technical context of canonical gravity research.

# The Instanton Representation of Plebanski Gravity: Consistency of the Constraint Surface Under Lagrangian Time Evolution

## Abstract

This paper examines the instanton representation of Plebanski gravity, a reformulation of general relativity built upon self-dual two-forms and an auxiliary field encoding the dynamical content of the gravitational field. The equations of motion of this theory consist of a Hodge self-duality condition on the field strength of a Yang–Mills-type connection together with a set of generalized Maxwell's equations, both of which are governed by the initial value constraints of general relativity — namely the Gauss law, the diffeomorphism (vector) constraint, and the Hamiltonian (scalar) constraint. A central question in any constrained dynamical system is whether the constraint surface defined by these conditions is preserved under time evolution, i.e., whether the constraints remain satisfied at all times once imposed on an initial hypersurface. In the present work we investigate this question directly at the level of the Lagrangian equations of motion, rather than through the conventional Dirac–Bergmann algorithm which proceeds via the Hamiltonian and the computation of Poisson brackets. We show explicitly that the constraint surface of the instanton representation is indeed preserved under this second-order, Lagrangian-based time evolution. The results are placed in the broader context of the Ashtekar formulation of gravity, to which the instanton representation is closely related, and the comparison reinforces the internal consistency of the instanton representation as a legitimate and self-contained formulation of the dynamics of general relativity.

## 1. Introduction

The search for reformulations of general relativity that render its dynamical structure more transparent has a long history, beginning with the Arnowitt–Deser–Misner (ADM) canonical formulation and continuing through the introduction of self-dual variables by Ashtekar. The Ashtekar formulation recasts general relativity as a theory of a complex $SO(3,\mathbb{C})$ (or $SU(2)$) connection and a conjugate densitized triad, in terms of which the Hamiltonian and diffeomorphism constraints take a polynomial form dramatically simpler than their ADM counterparts. This simplification opened new avenues both for canonical quantization programs, most notably loop quantum gravity, and for classical investigations of the geometric and topological structure of the gravitational phase space.

A further development in this direction is the Plebanski formulation, which describes gravity in terms of self-dual two-form fields subject to a set of algebraic constraints ensuring that these two-forms derive from a genuine tetrad. Building on this, the *instanton representation of Plebanski gravity* introduces an auxiliary field — often denoted $\Psi^{ae}$ — which encodes the same physical information as the ADM three-metric and extrinsic curvature, but organizes it in a manner naturally adapted to the self-dual connection. In this formulation, the dynamical equations of motion take the form of (i) a Hodge duality condition relating the field strength of the connection to the two-form fields through $\Psi^{ae}$, and (ii) a collection of generalized Maxwell-type equations governing the propagation of the electric field variables conjugate to the connection.

A crucial feature of any constrained field theory — and general relativity is a paradigmatic example of such a theory — is the requirement that the constraints defining the physical phase space be preserved under time evolution. In the standard canonical treatment, this requirement is analyzed through the Dirac–Bergmann algorithm: one computes the Poisson bracket of each constraint with the total Hamiltonian and demands that the result vanish (weakly), either identically or upon imposition of additional secondary constraints. For general relativity in Ashtekar variables, this procedure has been carried out extensively and is known to close consistently, reproducing the first-class constraint algebra characteristic of a diffeomorphism-invariant theory.

However, the instanton representation of Plebanski gravity, owing to the way in which it packages the gravitational degrees of freedom, admits an alternative and in some respects more direct route to establishing the same consistency: one may work entirely at the level of the *Lagrangian* equations of motion, examining whether the constraint surface — defined as the locus in field space where the Gauss law, diffeomorphism constraint, and Hamiltonian constraint all vanish — is left invariant by the second-order evolution equations derived from the action, without ever passing through the Legendre transform, the construction of the total Hamiltonian, or the computation of Poisson brackets. This approach is of interest both as an independent consistency check on the formalism and as a demonstration that the preservation of the constraint surface is, in this representation, a direct consequence of the structure of the equations of motion themselves.

## 2. The Instanton Representation and Its Equations of Motion

The instanton representation is constructed from an action functional involving a self-dual $SO(3,\mathbb{C})$ connection $A^a_i$, its associated field strength $F^a_{ij}$, and the auxiliary field $\Psi^{ae}$, which plays the role analogous to the inverse conformal three-metric density weighted appropriately, encoding the momentum content of the theory. Variation of the action with respect to the various fields yields two principal sets of equations:

**(i) The Hodge self-duality condition.** This equation states that the field strength $F^a_{ij}$, when suitably projected and combined with $\Psi^{ae}$, is self-dual with respect to the internal $SO(3,\mathbb{C})$ indices — a direct descendant of the self-duality condition on the two-forms in the original Plebanski action. This condition effectively determines the electric field (densitized triad) in terms of the magnetic field $B^{ai} = \tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon^{ijk}F^a_{jk}$ and $\Psi^{ae}$.

**(ii) The generalized Maxwell equations.** These equations govern the time evolution of the field strength itself, taking the schematic form of a Yang–Mills-type propagation equation sourced by covariant derivatives of $\Psi^{ae}$ and the connection. They generalize the vacuum Maxwell equations of electromagnetism to the non-Abelian, gravitationally coupled setting of the self-dual connection.

Both of these dynamical equations are constrained: their consistency and physical interpretation depend on the prior or simultaneous satisfaction of the initial value constraints of general relativity, namely:

- The **Gauss law constraint** $G^a \approx 0$, generating internal $SO(3,\mathbb{C})$ gauge rotations;
- The **diffeomorphism (vector) constraint** $H_i \approx 0$, generating spatial diffeomorphisms;
- The **Hamiltonian (scalar) constraint** $H \approx 0$, generating the dynamical evolution (up to diffeomorphisms) normal to the spatial hypersurface.

In the instanton representation, these three constraints, when expressed in terms of $\Psi^{ae}$ and the connection variables, take a form directly analogous to their Ashtekar counterparts, but with the additional structure imposed by the self-duality condition built into the definition of $\Psi^{ae}$ itself.

# The Plebański Formulation and the Hodge Star: A Bridge Between Geometry and Gravity

The Plebański formulation of general relativity represents one of the more elegant reformulations of Einstein's theory of gravity, recasting it in terms of self-dual two-forms rather than the traditional metric tensor. Developed by Jerzy Plebański in the 1970s, this approach has become particularly significant in the study of loop quantum gravity and other approaches to quantizing spacetime geometry. At the heart of this formulation lies a deep connection to the Hodge star operator, a mathematical tool that plays a crucial role in differential geometry.

The Hodge star operator, or Hodge duality, provides a way to map k-forms to (n-k)-forms on an n-dimensional manifold equipped with a metric. In four-dimensional Lorentzian or Riemannian geometry, this operator becomes especially interesting when applied to two-forms, since it maps two-forms back to two-forms. This self-referential property allows for the decomposition of the space of two-forms into self-dual and anti-self-dual components—eigenspaces of the Hodge star operator with eigenvalues of plus and minus one (or plus and minus i, depending on the signature of the metric).

Plebański's key insight was to reformulate gravity using these self-dual two-forms as the fundamental variables, rather than the metric itself. In this framework, the gravitational action is expressed through a set of two-forms and a Lagrange multiplier field that enforces certain algebraic constraints. When these constraints are satisfied, the two-forms can be shown to arise from a tetrad, or vierbein, from which the usual spacetime metric can be reconstructed. The self-duality condition, defined precisely through the action of the Hodge star, ensures that the resulting geometry satisfies Einstein's equations.

This reformulation offers several advantages. First, it simplifies the mathematical structure of general relativity by working with forms rather than the more complex metric tensor directly. Second, it provides a natural bridge to gauge theory formulations of gravity, since the self-dual two-forms can be associated with connections valued in the Lie algebra of SU(2) or similar gauge groups. This connection has proven invaluable for approaches like loop quantum gravity, where the Ashtekar variables—themselves closely related to the Plebański formulation—form the foundation for a background-independent quantization of the gravitational field.

The interplay between the Hodge star and the Plebański action also illuminates deeper aspects of four-dimensional geometry. The fact that the Hodge star operator has a nontrivial action on two-forms specifically in four dimensions is not a coincidence; it reflects the special role that four-dimensional spacetime plays in general relativity. This dimensional peculiarity is what allows the self-dual decomposition to exist in the first place, making the Plebański formulation intrinsically tied to the dimensionality of our universe.

In summary, the Plebański formulation demonstrates how sophisticated mathematical structures—particularly the Hodge star operator and the theory of differential forms—can provide powerful alternative descriptions of physical theories. By reframing gravity in terms of self-dual two-forms, this approach not only offers computational and conceptual advantages but also opens pathways toward a deeper understanding of quantum gravity, revealing connections between geometry, topology, and the fundamental forces of nature.

# Hodge Self-Duality, Generalized Maxwell Equations, and Gravitational Degrees of Freedom in Plebanski Gravity

## Abstract

We investigate the role of Hodge self-duality in the Plebanski formulation of general relativity, wherein gravitational dynamics are encoded in a triplet of self-dual two-forms subject to algebraic and differential constraints. By imposing self-duality with respect to an internal SU(2) structure, the Plebanski action reduces the independent gravitational degrees of freedom to a set of curvature two-forms satisfying equations structurally analogous to a non-Abelian generalization of Maxwell's equations. We demonstrate that the associated Bianchi identities and equations of motion can be recast in a language reminiscent of source-free electromagnetism, with the self-dual field strengths playing the role of generalized field tensors and the simplicity constraints enforcing the correct correspondence to a metric-compatible spacetime geometry. This construction clarifies the counting of physical degrees of freedom—two propagating polarizations of the graviton—by isolating the self-dual sector from the full set of two-form variables, mirroring the reduction achieved in Yang-Mills theory upon imposition of self-duality. We further examine the constraint structure governing the reality conditions and non-degeneracy of the associated soldering form, essential for recovering Lorentzian general relativity from the underlying complex or split-signature theory. Finally, we compare this formulation to the Ashtekar variables, showing that the Plebanski two-form action naturally reduces, upon partial gauge-fixing and solving the simplicity constraints, to the Ashtekar self-dual connection formulation of canonical gravity. This comparison highlights the deep interplay between self-duality, first-order geometric variables, and the non-perturbative quantization program initiated by Ashtekar, while emphasizing the advantages of the Plebanski framework in exhibiting the topological and BF-theoretic origins of gravitational dynamics.

We present a proof that the constraint surface arising in the initial value formulation of general relativity remains invariant under time evolution, establishing this result directly from the Lagrangian equations of motion rather than through the conventional Dirac-Bergmann Hamiltonian constraint analysis. Starting from the Arnowitt-Deser-Misner (ADM) decomposition of spacetime into spatial slices evolving in time, we identify the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints as consequences of the Gauss-Codazzi relations projected onto the spatial hypersurface. Rather than treating these constraints as arising from the degeneracy of the Legendre transform in a phase-space (Hamiltonian) framework, we work directly with the second-order Euler-Lagrange equations obtained from the Einstein-Hilbert action, together with the twice-contracted Bianchi identity, which encodes the differential conservation of the Einstein tensor. We show that this Bianchi identity, when projected appropriately using the normal vector to the spatial slices, yields an evolution equation for the constraint quantities themselves, demonstrating that if the constraints are satisfied on an initial slice, the Lagrangian evolution equations force them to remain satisfied on all later slices. This provides an alternative, geometrically transparent derivation of constraint propagation that bypasses the introduction of primary and secondary constraints, Poisson brackets, and the full apparatus of constrained Hamiltonian dynamics. The argument clarifies the role of the Bianchi identities as the underlying reason for constraint preservation, independent of the choice of canonical formalism, and offers a complementary perspective to the standard Dirac procedure by emphasizing the covariance and geometric origin of the constraints within the purely Lagrangian, spacetime-covariant treatment of Einstein's equations.
